content:
Epic Games has filed a response to Apple's request that the court order both parties into settlement talks. Details below.

Epic argues that court-ordered settlement talks would be pointless

On Thursday of last week, Apple submitted a proposal outlining the commission structure it would adopt for in-app purchases made through systems outside the App Store within the United States.

Under Apple's proposal, the company would charge up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems.

On the same day, Apple filed a separate motion asking Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

In its motion, Apple stated that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential and non-adversarial environment will increase the chances of reaching a pragmatic solution, thereby avoiding lengthy remand proceedings."

Epic has now responded to Apple's motion, stating that although the company "has always been and remains willing to accept any serious settlement proposal from Apple that introduces competition and benefits all developers," it "does not believe that referring the case to a settlement conference at this time will meaningfully increase the likelihood of reaching such a settlement."

Epic added in its response: "If the Court orders the case to be referred to a settlement conference, Epic will participate in good faith."

It is now up to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to decide whether to refer the case to a settlement conference. Apple has requested that any such conference be conducted under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.

Epic's full response is available below:

9to5Mac Opinion

Apple has repeatedly attempted to narrow the scope of Judge Gonzalez Rogers's injunction concerning transactions outside the App Store. Apple has argued in particular that, since Epic's case is not a class action, the injunction should not apply broadly to other developers.

For instance, in one of its appeals, Apple argued that developers seeking similar relief should file their own lawsuits rather than benefit from the injunction in Epic's case. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Apple's attempt to narrow the injunction's scope, ruling that limiting the injunction to Epic and its affiliates would fail to provide Epic with the complete relief it seeks.

This ruling is also consistent with the public position Epic has maintained throughout most of the case — that its fight is not limited to its own commercial interests, but aims to benefit developers more broadly.

In its motion requesting that the case be referred to (confidential) settlement talks, Apple did not indicate what proposal it might put forward. However, anyone closely following this case would likely agree that Apple is likely to seek a deal that is particularly attractive to Epic, while limiting any concessions to Epic alone.

In fact, Epic's response has pre-empted this argument, noting that any "serious settlement proposal" from Apple must "benefit all developers," and hinting at the end of its response that Apple's efforts may be too little, too late.

If you were Apple, what offer would you make to Epic Games? Let us know in the comments.
